sources.news_title: Canada's retaliatory tariffs hit US products as Trump warns of escalation - The Pulse of NH
sources.text:
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs hit US products as Trump warns of escalation
(WASHINGTON) -- Retaliatory tariffs issued by Canada hit some imports from the United States at one minute after midnight Eastern Time on Tuesday, intensifying a trade war between the longtime allies and risking an escalation from President Donald Trump.
Levies as high as 50% apply to hundreds of U.S. products, ranging from aluminum foil to raincoats to cheese. U.S. elected officials in states bordering Canada, including Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, have warned the trade dispute will hurt local businesses and consumers.
Canadian officials said the retaliatory measure would target about $20 billion worth of U.S. products, mirroring the size of a recent batch of U.S. levies. The targeted goods amount to nearly 6% of annual U.S. exports to Canada, according to U.S. Census Bureau data for 2025.
A tit-for-tat trade war erupted last month after official negotiations collapsed and a fresh round of U.S. levies took hold. Within days, Canadian officials announced what they described as matching tariffs that would begin in the second week of September.
The Canadian tariffs target many products included in a batch of U.S. levies last month.
Trump has repeatedly warned of a forceful response if the Canadian tariffs were to take hold.
On Monday afternoon, Trump threatened to bar the sale of planes made by Canada-based aerospace company Bombardier unless the firm agreed to manufacture products in the U.S.
"If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank,'" Trump wrote in a social media post.
In a statement to ABC News, Bombardier said it generates jobs and other economic benefits in the U.S.
"The American aerospace industry is a clear winner on trade and exports. Bombardier is a strong contributor to the sector, creating tens of thousands of jobs across the United States. Aerospace is routinely one of the top export sectors for the United States and a continual trade surplus winner," the statement said in part.
Late last month, Trump vowed to ratchet up tariffs from 25% to 50% on Canadian-made cars and auto parts beginning in January.
"On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with," Trump said on his social media platform at the time. "They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!"
Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 27 changing the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America." Days later, Trump posted on social media an AI-generated video of birds with Trump's signature hairstyle marching with firearms to protect a body of water labeled "Lake America."
Canada said it will continue referring to the lake as "Lake Ontario." In a post on X late last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said, "This lake is called Lake Ontario -- today and forever."
Carney rebuked the Trump administration further last week, saying U.S. public messaging signaled an unwillingness to negotiate a resolution.
"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney said.
In the first half of 2026, the U.S. exported $175.8 billion in goods to Canada -- the second-biggest export trading partner after Mexico -- accounting for 14% of all U.S. exports, according to the Census Bureau.
For now, levies apply to a sliver of goods that travel between the U.S. and Canada, limiting the impact of the trade dispute, but a potential escalation threatens to deepen the pain for both economies.
"This is a classic trade-war situation: Somebody puts on a tariff, another country retaliates dollar for dollar and then more tariffs are added," Campbell Harvey, a professor at Duke's Fuqua School of Business who studies commodity markets, previously told ABC News. "Then we get into this really bad equilibrium."

sources.news_title: Canadian tariffs on U.S. milk, perfume, golf clubs and other goods take effect as trade war grinds on - RAW CHILI
sources.text:
Canada’s steep retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion in U.S. goods took effect just after midnight ET on Tuesday, extending the trade war between the two countries.
The Canadian government announced the planned tariffs two weeks ago, after trade negotiations broke down and the Trump administration followed through on a threat to impose 50% duties on $20 billion worth of goods from Canada. Officials in Canada have vowed to match the U.S. levies “dollar for dollar.”
Canada’s tariffs range from 15% to 50%. American milk, perfume, video game consoles, golf clubs, fishing rods, steel, aluminum, jackets and T-shirts will face 50% tariffs. Cheese, carpets and certain household appliances like stoves and air conditioners will be subject to 25% tariffs, and forklifts and industrial molds will face 15% tariffs.
Initially, some American seafood was slated to face 25% tariffs, but Canada removed those tariffs from the list following pushback from the lobster industry.
Economists say Canada’s tariffs could hit manufacturers in Midwestern states like Michigan and Indiana particularly hard, as well as dairy producers in Wisconsin and Vermont.
The levies were imposed in response to U.S. tariffs on Canadian milk, honey, hockey sticks, alcoholic beverages, plywood, down feathers, jewelry and other goods.
The tit-for-tat tariffs impact a small fraction of the goods that flow across the U.S.-Canada border, which totaled more than $700 billion last year, according to U.S. government figures. But they mark an escalation in an increasingly bitter trade dispute between the two allies.
President Trump threatened hefty tariffs on Canadian and Mexican goods shortly after returning to office last year, in response to what he said he viewed as insufficient action to prevent drugs and migrants from crossing into the United States. Canada reacted with its own retaliatory measures, including tariffs on U.S. goods and boycotts on American liquor in some provinces.
The two sides later launched trade talks and called off some of their most stringent measures, but tensions have remained high. Mr. Trump chose not to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement — a deal he inked during his first term — beyond 2036. The two countries have also feuded over NATO and Mr. Trump’s musings about making Canada the 51st U.S. state.
Over the summer, the Trump administration threatened tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods, accusing Canada of discriminating against American-made goods and retaliating excessively against Mr. Trump’s 2025 trade measures.
Mr. Trump briefly delayed those tariffs last month as U.S. and Canadian negotiators neared a deal, but they were ultimately unable to reach an agreement. Both sides accused each other of torpedoing the negotiations by tacking on last-minute demands.
After pulling out of talks, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has argued the Trump administration “asked too much and offered too little,” and pressed for control over Canada’s trade deals with other countries — an arrangement he cast as a threat to the country’s sovereignty. He also said the U.S.’ “signature was written in pencil” on prior deals.
Mr. Trump, meanwhile, has accused Canada of unfair trade practices and claimed it “wants the benefits of being a State, without being one.”
“I don’t want Canadian cars, I don’t want Canadian parts, I don’t want Canadian anything,” Mr. Trump wrote last month on social media. “They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop.”
As the war of words escalated, Ontario Premier Doug Ford — who leads Canada’s largest province — called Mr. Trump a “dictator” and said he can “kiss my a**” last month. Mr. Trump later moved to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The U.S. president has suggested additional tariffs and trade restrictions could be on the way. Last month, he announced 50% tariffs on all Canadian automotive and steel imports starting in January. And on Monday, he pushed for an end to imports of Bombardier planes unless the Montreal-based company moves production to the United States.

With the trade war between the North American neighbors heating up, new Canadian duties apply to $27.6 billion (US$20 billion) in US imports, covering steel and aluminum products as well as dairy goods like cheese.
“We have everything we need to pivot and prosper,” Carney said. “That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still.”
Ottawa’s pushback comes after President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a similar value of Canadian products, over what Washington deemed as “discriminatory treatment” against US alcohol, automobile and dairy industries.
On Monday, Trump threatened to try to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation in the United States unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the US.

– ‘Get up, governor’ –
“I don’t believe in escalating the conflict. That’s not constructive,” Carney said in his video statement Tuesday. “But our tariffs are necessary to protect our workers, protect our companies, and our communities.
“This is about who we are as Canadians. It’s about our livelihoods and the country that we leave to our kids.”

Trump also signed an order in August to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as “Lake America” — sparking fury in Canada amid a broader wave of patriotism triggered by the US president’s hostility.
Although Carney is backed by Canadian public opinion, his country remains reliant on its neighbor. Nearly 60 percent of Canada’s imports come from the United States and about 70 percent of its exports go to the US market.
To help businesses and workers, Canada’s government has unveiled an aid package of $7.5 billion (US$5.4 billion).

sources.news_title: Canada's $20 billion in retaliatory tariffs hit the US on September 8, but most of the cost falls on domestic buyers
sources.text:
Canada’s new counter-tariffs took effect at 12:01 a.m. on September 8, 2026. According to the Department of Finance tariff schedule, duties of 15%, 25%, and 50% apply to C$27.6 billion in US-origin imports. That is approximately US$20 billion.
The measures cover steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics, and hundreds of other product classifications. Al Jazeera reported that the tariffs took effect after trade negotiations failed and identified Mark Carney, not Justin Trudeau, as Canada’s prime minister.
The tariffs respond to US duties imposed on Canadian goods in August. Ottawa describes its response as dollar-for-dollar and rate-for-rate, meaning the Canadian measures are intended to match the value and rates of the American action.
That does not mean the money is initially collected from American exporters. Canadian customs authorities collect the tariff from the importer bringing the affected product into Canada. The importer can absorb the added cost, ask suppliers for concessions, switch sources, or pass some of the expense along through higher prices.
The 96% figure in the original framing came from a January 2026 Kiel Institute policy brief. Using shipment-level data covering almost $4 trillion in trade, its authors concluded that foreign exporters absorbed about 4% of the 2025 US tariff burden while the remaining 96% passed through to US buyers.
That is strong evidence against the claim that foreign countries simply pay another government’s tariffs. It is not, however, a measurement of Canada’s September 2026 counter-tariffs. Applying the exact 96% figure to a different country, tariff schedule, and period would create false precision.
The more directly relevant evidence comes from a 2026 Bank of Canada staff working paper examining Canadian retaliatory tariffs introduced in March 2025. It found that retail prices for tariffed goods rose gradually and peaked about 6% higher after three months, representing roughly one-quarter pass-through from the 25% tariff to retail prices.
The researchers also found little systematic decline in the prices received by US exporters. That suggests foreign suppliers absorbed only a limited part of the burden, although the paper could not divide the remaining cost precisely among Canadian importers, wholesalers, retailers, and consumers.
The defensible conclusion is therefore broader than the original 96% claim. Most of the economic burden is likely to remain inside the country imposing the tariff, but consumers may not see the entire tariff rate added immediately to the shelf price. Businesses can absorb part of it through lower margins, draw down existing inventory, change suppliers, or delay price increases.
Retaliation is still a domestic economic cost used for a foreign-policy purpose. It has a political target abroad, but much of its financial pressure appears at home.
Canada’s decision is not cost-free, and Ottawa’s own response acknowledges that. The government’s August 25 announcement included C$7.5 billion in new and expanded support for workers and businesses affected by the trade dispute.
The package includes additional regional support for small and medium-sized companies, new liquidity through the Business Development Bank of Canada, funding for diversification projects, and assistance for affected workers and employers. It builds on nearly C$25 billion in support the government says it had already provided since the US tariff measures began.
The package does not establish exactly how much of the tariff burden consumers will pay. It does show that Ottawa expects Canadian companies and workers to experience significant disruption while the counter-tariffs remain in place.
The product rules also matter. The tariffs apply to specified US-origin goods, and products already in transit when the measures took effect are exempt. That is more precise than saying every border crossing automatically creates another tariff charge.
Integrated supply chains remain especially exposed because a tariffed component can increase the cost of a finished product assembled elsewhere. Whether that increase reaches the consumer depends on the product’s origin, its tariff classification, available exemptions, inventory levels, and how much of the cost each company can absorb.
American buyers face the same basic mechanism under the US tariffs on Canadian goods. US importers pay those duties at the border, after which the cost can move through wholesalers, manufacturers, retailers, and eventually households. The final pass-through can vary by industry and by how long businesses expect the dispute to continue.
That expectation matters. The Bank of Canada researchers found that firms anticipating longer-lasting tariffs planned to pass through more of the cost than firms expecting the measures to disappear sooner. A temporary political warning and a durable trade barrier can therefore produce different pricing decisions even when the tariff rate is identical.
The September 8 measures do not prove that the US-Canada trade framework has legally ended. They do show that the existing framework is no longer containing the dispute as effectively as businesses on either side of the border once assumed.
For households, the consequences are likely to emerge unevenly. Some prices may rise quickly, some businesses may accept lower margins, and some importers may abandon US suppliers altogether. The clearest evidence available does not justify assigning 96% of Canada’s new tariff burden to domestic buyers, but it does show why Canadians should not expect the cost to remain on the other side of the border.
The tariffs are aimed at Washington. Much of their economic weight will still land in Canada.

sources.news_title: New Canadian counter-tariffs reach mining and industrial supply chains
sources.text:
OTTAWA — Canada’s latest counter-tariffs on U.S. goods are now in effect, covering everything from dairy products and household appliances to industrial machinery, steel products and equipment used in mining and the oilpatch.
The tariffs took effect at 12:01 a.m. Monday and apply at rates of 15, 25 and 50 per cent to $27.6 billion worth of imports from the United States. The federal government says the measures match U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar and rate for rate.
The new measures follow the United States imposing a 50 per cent tariff on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods on Aug. 22.
Ottawa’s complete list of U.S. products subject to counter-tariffs reaches across hundreds of tariff classifications, with the federal government identifying steel and aluminum, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics among the sectors targeted.
Food products include numerous forms of milk and cream, whey products and cheeses, along with natural honey and some baking mixes and doughs. Consumer products range from refrigerators and washing machines to cosmetics and other household goods.
The list also reaches deeply into industrial supply chains, including products and components used in mining, construction and the energy sector.
Among them are steel pipes and fittings, some fittings specifically intended for mining and oil and gas applications, grinding balls used in mills and components used in oil and natural gas development.
Heavy equipment components are also included, such as buckets, shovels, grabs and grips, bulldozer and angledozer blades, and parts for boring or sinking machinery.
Other industrial products facing tariffs include hydraulic jacks and hoists, cranes, forklifts and other loading and material-handling equipment.
The measures extend into Canada’s transportation and shipping supply chains.
Commercial freight trailers and semi-trailers are included, along with farm and logging freight wagons and trailers for logging trucks.
Railway equipment is also covered, including some railway maintenance vehicles and components such as axles, wheels, brakes and coupling equipment.
Packaging and transportation products on the list include cartons and boxes, sacks and bags, steel tanks and drums, and some transportation containers.
The federal government says the counter-tariffs are intended to put Canadian producers affected by U.S. tariffs on a more competitive footing against American products sold in Canada.
Some steel and aluminum products that were already subject to 25 per cent Canadian counter-tariffs are now subject to a 50 per cent rate, while other existing counter-tariffs, including those on U.S. automobiles, remain in place.
Goods already in transit to Canada when the new measures took effect are exempt from the latest counter-tariffs.

sources.news_title: Canada imposes $20b tariffs on US goods
sources.text:
Canada struck back at US President Donald Trump on Tuesday with tariffs on about $20 billion worth of US goods, in response to the latest round of tariffs on Canada.
The outcome could resonate far beyond Canada, showing other governments whether a smaller US ally can withstand Trump’s economic pressure.
Republicans will descend on Dallas this week for a two-day convention dreamed up by Trump to rally his supporters for this year’s midterm elections. Republicans have never held a midterm convention before, although Democrats did in the 1970s and 1980s.
Americans’ satisfaction with the quality of K-12 education in the country has hit a low point. Just 32 per cent of American adults say they are “completely” or “somewhat” satisfied with the US school system, according to a new poll.
That’s an 11-point drop over the past two years and the lowest since Gallup began polling on the subject 27 years ago.

sources.news_title: Retaliatory Tariffs Will Raise Costs For Consumers
sources.text:
The trade war between Canada and the United States has officially kicked into high gear after high stakes talks between the two countries collapsed last weekend.
President Donald Trump’s escalated tariffs came into effect on Saturday and a series of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Cabinet members unveiled roughly $27.6 billion in counter-tariffs on Tuesday, to take effect on Sept. 8.
In the weeks leading up to the collapse of trade talks, Canadian politicians took to U.S. airwaves, warning that Trump’s plans to increase tariffs on Canadian goods entering the United States would backfire by raising costs for U.S. consumers.
“A tariff on Canada is a tax on the American people,” said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on American television just last weekend.
Those politicians, like Ford, were right.
Unfortunately, the federal government has chosen to respond to Trump’s tariffs by introducing tens of billions of dollars of tariffs of its own, which will only serve to raise costs for Canadian consumers.
“When the United States asked too much and offered too little, we chose to stand up for Canadians,” said Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne. “Our dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs as well as a multi-billion-dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses as a we build a stronger, more resilient, and more diversified economy.”
But anyone who believes that tariffs are the solution to Canada’s trade problems, not to mention the present cost-of-living crisis, is kidding themselves.

sources.news_title: Canada Escalates Trade Dispute with U.S.
sources.text:
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect shortly after midnight Tuesday, as Prime Minister Mark Carney increased economic pressure on the country’s largest trading partner following the collapse of negotiations last month.
The move intensifies an 18-month-old trade dispute between the two neighbours.
The counter-tariffs cover about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods, with duties ranging from 15% to 50% on products including steel, furniture, clothing and electronics.
The dollar-for-dollar response marks a further escalation, with officials on both sides blaming each other for the breakdown of talks that had appeared close to a deal two weeks earlier.
The dispute is also raising concerns about the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement (USMCA), which faces annual reviews after U.S. President Donald Trump declined to extend the pact for another decade.
“What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral,” said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney’s advisory committee on bilateral U.S. economic relations. “But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage,” Harvey said.
Pressure on Canadian Industries
Trump’s tariffs introduced last month targeted several Canadian sectors, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment. The measures cover approximately $20 billion, or 5%, of Canadian exports to the U.S.
Canada remains heavily dependent on the U.S. market, with almost 68% of its exports going south of the border this year. Roughly 80% of those exports have moved duty-free under the USMCA, providing some protection for the Canadian economy.
However, the latest U.S. tariffs, imposed under a Depression-era law, do not permit Ottawa to rely on those USMCA exemptions.
ALSO READ: U.S. Imposes 50% Tariffs as Canada Trade Talks Collapse
The uncertainty surrounding the trade agreement has raised concerns about investment and economic growth, particularly as Canada confronts an economy roughly 13 times its size.
While Carney continues to enjoy broad public support, political analysts warn that prolonged economic disruption could weaken that support.
Public opinion in the United States also appears divided, with only 20% of Americans approving of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Carney said last week that Canada remained prepared to negotiate a trade agreement that benefits both countries. However, Trump has also threatened to raise U.S. tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks and automotive parts to 50% from January 1.
For now, formal discussions appear to have stalled. A Canadian government source said there are currently no talks between ministers or government officials from the two countries.
“The Canadian government needs to keep channels open to the United States and not go overboard in terms of rhetoric and reacting to the rhetoric from the American side, while waiting for the American decision-making process to come back to economics,” Harvey said.
Reuters

sources.news_title: Canada's Retaliatory Tariffs Take Effect, and Bigger Threats Loom
sources.text:
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on the US took effect at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, covering $27.6 billion in American goods at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%, varying by product. The measures match the US’s own 50% tariffs on Canadian goods dollar for dollar, hitting more than 700 products across sectors like dairy, agricultural equipment, aluminum, steel and household appliances.
Steel and aluminum tariffs doubled to 50% under the new measures, bringing Canada’s rate in line with what the US already charges on those same Canadian metals, and goods already en route to Canada when the deadline hit are exempt.
Read: Canada Matches U.S. Levies with $27.6B in Counter-Tariffs
One item on that list stands out for how ordinary it is — toilet paper. No country ships more of it to the US than Canada does. US-based mills aren’t insulated either — Canadian softwood pulp accounts for close to a third of the fiber in a typical American-made roll, so the tariffs hit that supply chain twice, once on the raw pulp and once on the finished product. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has downplayed the risk, putting Canadian imports at just 0.06% of what Americans consume and adding that “there’s no possible way it can really affect US well-being.”
Read: Canada’s Tariffs Threaten a Repeat of America’s Covid-Era Toilet Paper Panic
Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose the original US duties, arguing Canadian practices around alcohol, dairy, and vehicles unfairly disadvantaged American businesses. On Canada’s side, only products that trace their origin to the US under Canada’s marking regulations get hit with the new duties. Importers pay the cost at the border, then decide whether to absorb it or pass it on to customers.
Washington’s own 50% tariffs on Canadian goods took effect August 22, hours after Carney walked away from the table over last-minute changes Washington made to the deal.
Read: What Washington Really Demanded Before Canada Walked Away
The rejected framework would have brought steel duties down to 25% on a set quota of Canadian shipments, cut the aluminum rate in half to 25%, and eliminated a 10% tariff on softwood lumber. In exchange, Canada would have dropped its retaliatory auto tariffs, loosened dairy supply-management rules and ended provincial boycotts of American alcohol.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly intervened late in the negotiations, pushing to keep aluminum out of any tariff relief and narrow the auto concessions so they wouldn’t cover medium- and heavy-duty trucks — changes that would have hit General Motors‘ Oshawa plant and Ford‘s planned Oakville retool. Some analysts have since argued the rejected deal may have been better for Canada than the trade war that replaced it.
Read: Trump escalates Canada trade war with 50% auto tariffs
Prime Minister Mark Carney has cast the response as reluctant, saying some US companies and states are “innocent bystanders” in a trade dispute they didn’t choose. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne struck a harder note, saying the US tariffs “will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses, and communities across our nation.”
Read: Carney Says US Wanted to ‘Wipe Out’ Canadian Industries in Trade Talks
Trump has kept a personal edge on the dispute throughout. After Carney accused US negotiators of demanding French-language concessions in the failed talks, Trump dismissed the claim as a lie invented “to gain political support” in Quebec. He has threatened to extend the 50% tariff rate to Canadian vehicles and auto parts starting January 1, 2027. The same week, he moved to bar Bombardier from selling in the US entirely unless it builds aircraft domestically, a threat Quebec’s premier and a Republican Kansas senator have both pushed back on.
Trump also went further than rhetoric once already, putting his signature on an order in late August that rebrands Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” “This is official, effective immediately,” he said at the signing, adding that he’d already filed the necessary paperwork. The change only governs how the US federal government refers to the lake and carries no weight over Canada or international usage, but Carney fired back on social media, noting the lake’s centuries-old Indigenous name predates both countries and that “naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Read: Trump Personally Called Apple to Rename Lake Ontario
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has renewed his threat to cut off Canadian electricity exports to the US if the trade war keeps escalating — the province supplies power to New York, Michigan and Minnesota. Acting alone wouldn’t be enough, he said, calling for a “Team Canada approach” from the other provinces that also export power south.
Canada’s new duties touch roughly 6% of what it buys from the US, and the US tariffs that triggered them cover about 5% of what America buys from Canada. Alongside the tariffs, Ottawa is putting $7.5 billion toward supporting Canadian businesses and workers hurt by the trade war.
Trump’s approval rating has slid to 33% in recent polling, matching the weakest reading Reuters/Ipsos has recorded for him. A separate poll from the same firm found little enthusiasm for the fight — only one in five Americans backed raising tariffs on Canada, while 57% opposed doing so.

sources.news_title: Canada’s tariff retaliation marks sharp new turn in trade war with US
sources.text:
Canada begins levying retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars of American goods today, the sharpest escalation yet in a trade war between two allies that once prided themselves on frictionless commerce.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will impose duties ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on C$27.6 billion, roughly US$20 billion, worth of American imports. The figure is no accident. It matches, almost to the dollar, the 50 per cent tariffs Washington slapped on Canadian exports on August 22. There is a certain irony in the timing too. A year ago Carney had quietly dismantled the counter-tariffs his predecessor Justin Trudeau had put in place, betting that patience would eventually be rewarded with a deal. That has now been abandoned.
The immediate trigger was the breakdown of negotiations in Washington late last month. Carney walked away from terms he called unfair and uneconomic. Much of the friction centred, oddly enough, on Quebec's French-language protections, which American negotiators treated as a mere business irritant and Canadian officials treated as non-negotiable. The blame game that followed was predictably one-sided. US Trade Representative Jameson Greer accused Canada of suspending talks for no good economic reason, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick suggested Carney had walked out simply to score points at home. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added his own note of condescension, arguing that an economy a thirteenth the size of America's had no business picking a tariff fight at all.
Ottawa's response suggests it disagrees. The retaliatory list covers around 700 American products. Tariffs on many steel items double from 25 to 50 per cent, and the net widens to catch aluminium foil, dairy, cheese, cosmetics, motorcycles, household appliances, paper goods, railway locomotives and electronics. Some minor US exports are also targeted, such as fish egg incubators and the metal bands attaching erasers to pencils. The targeting is deliberate. Michigan and Ohio, both heavily dependent on Canadian trade and both hosting closely watched midterm races in November, will feel the pinch first.
The dispute has drifted well beyond tariff schedules into territory that would seem farcical were the stakes not so real. Trump has once again taken to renaming places. On August 27, he signed an executive order rechristening Lake Ontario as Lake America, prompting Carney to retort that the lake is called Ontario today and will remain so. Trump followed with an AI-generated video of armed birds defending his lake, then posted a map showing the American flag draped over Canada and Greenland, and another striking out New Mexico in favour of New America. The last provoked a sharp rebuke from Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, who made clear her state's identity was not up for negotiation. Carney's own response was characteristically dry, telling Washington to stop posting memes and start being serious.
The confrontation reached a new pitch yesterday when Trump threatened to ban Bombardier from the American market altogether unless the Montreal-based aerospace manufacturer shifted production south of the border. He accused the company of living off American buyers while Canada shut out US banks and firms. Bombardier's rebuttal was arithmetic rather than rhetorical, pointing to 3,500 jobs across Kansas and Texas, billions spent with 2,800 American suppliers and half its global fleet flown by US customers. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette weighed in firmly, insisting no outside power would dictate where the province's companies chose to manufacture.
The strain is being felt closer to the ground too. Tim Tierney, Ottawa's deputy mayor and head of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, warned that local governments and residents would absorb the economic damage before anyone in Washington or Ottawa did. Public sentiment has already found small, symbolic outlets. Ottawa's city council voted unanimously to rename a street called Trump Avenue, a gesture more theatrical than substantive but telling nonetheless.
Economists see a deeper risk in all this than bruised feelings. North American auto supply chains are tightly integrated, and Canada remains the largest export market for American cars. Should that fail, Canadian buyers may simply turn to cheaper vehicles from elsewhere, most plausibly China. A trade war meant to teach Canada a lesson could end up handing Beijing an opening neither Ottawa nor Washington intended to create.

sources.news_title: Trump Watch: Trump trade war with Canada gets worse
sources.text:
Donald Trump matters a lot to Mzansi and the rest of the world right now. Trump is changing the way America works – and how the world’s most powerful country deals with the rest of the world.
We’ll track what he does and connect the dots to your daily life.
Trump trade war with Canada gets worse
Donald Trump’s trade fight with Canada has grown after Canada placed new taxes on billions of dollars of US goods.
Canada’s new tariffs took effect on Tuesday and cover almost C$28-billion worth of American products.
Some of the tariffs are as high as 50%. They apply to goods including steel, furniture and clothing.
Canada brought in the tariffs after Trump placed new taxes on Canadian products such as cars, steel, aluminium, dairy and alcohol.
Trump has also threatened to stop US business with Canadian aircraft company Bombardier unless it moves manufacturing to the US.
Trade talks between the two countries broke down in August. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada was ready to return to talks when the US was ready.
Trump has also criticised Canada’s currency and posted a map showing Canada covered by the US flag.
The US and Canada do nearly $900-billion in trade with each other. Businesses on both sides are now preparing for the fight to continue.
Image source: File
Trump plans calls with Putin and Zelenskyy
US President Donald Trump plans to speak by phone with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday.
Trump is expected to speak to Putin first and then Zelenskyy, according to a US official.
The calls are expected after Trump receives an update from his envoys about the latest talks on the war in Ukraine.
Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on 6 September for talks with Zelenskyy.
After the first round of talks, Kushner said Trump was determined to bring the war to an end.
Zelenskyy said several rounds of talks would take place in Kyiv, including meetings involving France, the UK and Germany.
Witkoff and Kushner left Kyiv by train during the night of 6 to 7 September.
Image source: File
Trump gets his face on new US coin
Donald Trump has become the first living US president in 100 years to appear on American currency.
The US Mint released a special $1 coin featuring Trump’s face on Wednesday to mark America’s 250th anniversary.
The coin shows Trump alongside the words “LIBERTY” and “IN GOD WE TRUST”.
The coins went on sale in rolls of 25 for $61 and bags of 100 for $154.50. They were listed as out of stock online within hours.
Despite their gold colour, the coins do not contain real gold. They are mostly made from copper.
US law stops living people from appearing on paper money. But the Trump government says the law does not clearly stop a living president from appearing on the front of a coin.
The last living US president to appear on a coin was Calvin Coolidge in 1926.
Trump’s government has also previously announced plans for a $250 note featuring his face, but that would need a change in the law.
Image source: US Treasury
Trump says he will not force Iran peace talks
US President Donald Trump says he is not trying to force Iran back into peace talks.
Trump made the comment as the US carried out another round of attacks on Iran.
He said America had almost total control of the Strait of Hormuz and claimed Iran’s economy was falling apart.
Trump also asked when the Iranian people would rise up against their government.
The US military said it hit air defence sites, communication systems and radar equipment in Iran.
Iran then fired missiles at Jordan, which is a US ally. Jordan said it stopped 10 of 13 missiles and that no one was killed or injured.
Bahrain also said it stopped Iranian attacks.
Oil prices rose again after the new fighting, with Brent crude reaching more than $94 a barrel.
Image source: File
Trump wins fight over White House ballroom
Donald Trump has won a major court battle over his $400-million White House ballroom.
The US Supreme Court ruled that construction can continue while a legal fight over the project carries on.
The court voted 5 to 4 to block lower court decisions that would have stopped part of the building work.
Trump demolished the historic East Wing last year to make way for the ballroom. The White House says the project should be mostly finished by November.
Chief Justice John Roberts disagreed with the ruling. He said the construction was likely unlawful because Congress had not approved it.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation brought the case. It argued that Trump did not have the power to make such major changes on his own.
Trump said he was pleased with the decision and called the lawsuit baseless.
The ballroom is part of a wider Trump plan to change parts of Washington, including a new helipad and other major building projects.
Image source: File
Trump orders strikes on Iran after month long pause
US President Donald Trump’s government has attacked Iran again after a break of more than a month.
The US military said it hit two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran said two people were killed and two others were injured in the strikes.
The US said the attack was limited and aimed at forces that were preparing to place mines in the strait.
Iran then said it fired missiles at US bases in Jordan. Jordan said it stopped eight missiles.
Iran also claimed it attacked a US-linked air base in the UAE with drones. The UAE denied the base had been hit but said it shot down one drone.
The strike was the first known US attack on Iran since Trump paused the military campaign in late July.
Trump later posted videos showing explosions at Iranian oil sites and repeated his warning that any boats laying new mines in the Strait of Hormuz would be destroyed.
Image source: File
Trump Iran war leaves US Navy short of money
Donald Trump’s war with Iran has pushed the US Navy into a serious money shortage.
Documents seen by the Guardian say the Navy has moved money from staff pay and other accounts to help cover the cost of the fighting.
The war began on 28 February. The Navy helped with the first attacks and has also been involved in the blockade of Iranian ports.
A Pentagon document warned that there were now shortages in payroll accounts because money had been moved to pay for military operations.
Navy officials said money is being moved between different budgets so sailors can still be paid. Some non-urgent repairs at Navy bases have also reportedly been delayed.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said in July that the Iran war had already cost $35.7-billion. The Trump government later asked Congress for another $67-billion for the military.
But it is unclear whether Congress will approve the extra money because the war has become unpopular.
The US Navy said it was still able to pay its staff and continue operations.
Image source: File
Trump says he is in no rush for Iran talks
US President Donald Trump says he has no deadline for Iran to return to talks.
“I’m not in a hurry,” Trump told Al Jazeera. He said the US would keep up the pressure for as long as needed.
Trump said America was “winning very big” and pointed to Iran’s rising prices and weak economy.
He also said both sanctions and military attacks were working against Iran.
The war will reach six months on Friday. Trump had earlier said the conflict could be over within weeks.
The US and Iran signed a temporary deal in June, but it expired earlier this month.
Trump’s government has now brought in stronger sanctions against Iran and companies in other countries that do business with Tehran.
Iran says the new sanctions break international rules. Its currency has also fallen sharply, making food and other basic goods much more expensive.
Image source: File
Iran media threatens Trump son Barron
Iranian state-linked media has shared a video threatening Donald Trump’s son Barron.
The video claimed to show where the 20-year-old lives and studies in New York. It also claimed to know details about his online accounts and some of his classmates.
Reports also claimed a $10-million bounty had been placed on Barron’s head. But the article said this could not be independently confirmed.
The video ended with the warning: “Barron Trump, wait for us.” It was shared by media linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Similar videos have also targeted Trump and his wife Melania. One earlier clip claimed to know Melania’s location.
Another video claimed to show routes used by Trump’s presidential convoy in Florida and New York.
Image source: File
Trump plans to cancel visas for asylum seekers
Donald Trump’s government plans to cancel some US visas held by foreigners who have applied for asylum.
The move would affect people who entered the US on short-term business or tourist visas and then asked to stay as asylum seekers.
The US State Department said it was working with immigration officials to identify those people and cancel their visas.
The government did not say how many people would be affected. But reports say up to 200,000 visas could be cancelled.
The visas involved are known as B1 and B2 visas. They are normally given to people travelling to the US for business or tourism.
Losing the visa would not automatically mean someone is deported. People with asylum cases still being considered could remain in the system, but would lose their business or tourist visa status.
Trump has made immigration one of the main focuses of his second term. His government says the crackdown is needed to improve security.
Rights groups say parts of the crackdown have treated some people unfairly and have raised concerns about racial profiling and legal rights.
Image source: File
Trump says aliens are living in the ocean
Donald Trump reportedly told someone close to him that mysterious beings are living in the ocean.
The claim comes from Jack Osbourne, the son of late rock star Ozzy Osbourne, the Daily Star reported.
Osbourne said he has a friend who speaks to Trump every week. He said the friend asked Trump about UFOs and aliens.
According to Osbourne, Trump replied: “We have no idea what they are, but they’re in the ocean.”
Trump has not publicly confirmed making the comment.
Osbourne said he found the claim interesting because large parts of the ocean have never been explored.
He said he believes some strange beings may be watching humans, but admitted he is still partly sceptical about stories involving aliens.
Trump has previously released government information about UFOs after promising more openness about the issue.
Image source: File
Trump says Iran was weeks away from nuclear weapon
US President Donald Trump says Iran was only weeks away from getting a new nuclear weapon when he ordered US strikes in 2025.
Trump said Iran had been working towards nuclear weapons for more than 50 years.
He claimed Iran had become a major threat in the Middle East and could have attacked Israel and other countries.
Trump said Iran was “exactly two weeks away” from having a new nuclear weapon when he ordered the strikes.
He said that was why the US had to act and stop Iran from getting such a weapon.
The US military attacked Iran’s Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan nuclear sites in June 2025.
The strikes used B-2 stealth bombers and powerful bombs designed to hit targets deep underground.
Trump said other US presidents and countries should have dealt with Iran’s nuclear plans earlier.
Image source: File
Trump threatens countries that keep doing business with Iran
US President Donald Trump has announced a new plan to put more economic pressure on Iran.
Trump said any country that helps Iran or does business with it could face major economic punishment from the US.
He said this could include countries whose banks, businesses, airports or government bodies help Iran.
Trump did not explain exactly what punishment would be used or which countries could be targeted.
The US has already placed many sanctions on Iran and is trying to stop the country from selling oil.
Trump also said activities such as oil smuggling, cash transfers and the use of fake companies must stop.
The move could create new tension with China, which is Iran’s biggest trading partner and buys Iranian oil.
Iran said sanctions and military pressure would not force it to give in, but said it was still open to talks with the US.
Image source: @WhiteHouse
Trump says Iran talks are off
US President Donald Trump says there are no talks planned with Iran and that a US naval blockade remains in place.
Trump also said the Strait of Hormuz was open and operating, and that all sea mines had been removed or destroyed.
Iran disagreed. A senior Iranian official said the strait would stay closed until the US followed the terms of an agreement signed in June.
Iran wants the US to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, remove oil sanctions, release frozen Iranian money and stop military attacks and threats.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner had said a day earlier that talks between the US and Iran were still happening.
Trump then said there were no talks taking place and none had been scheduled.
Attempts to reach a peace deal have now stalled. The war began when the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.
A senior Iranian official said Iran could now move to a more aggressive military approach because talks had failed.
Image source: File
Trump tells rescued boy he probably would not have saved him
US President Donald Trump has told a 10-year-old boy who nearly drowned that he probably would not have saved him.
Trump made the comment while honouring 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams at the White House.
Ryder rescued Nathaniel Rai after the boy was swept into deep water at a beach in California last month.
Video showed Ryder swimming into rough waves, grabbing Nathaniel and fighting his way back to shore.
Trump praised Ryder as a hero and said he would receive a high civilian honour.
But Trump then joked that Nathaniel was lucky he had not been the lifeguard that day.
“I don’t know if I’d do it. I wouldn’t, probably,” Trump said.
Ryder said he relied on his training during the rescue and hoped people would try to help others whenever they could.
Image source: File
Trump cuts South Korea drills after praising Kim Jong Un
US President Donald Trump says the US will reduce military exercises with South Korea.
Trump said the drills cost too much and sent the wrong message to North Korea.
He also pointed to his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The US and South Korea were due to start their yearly military exercises on Monday. Trump said it was too late to cancel them completely, but future drills would be reduced.
Trump also criticised South Korea for refusing to join the US in its efforts against Iran’s nuclear programme.
South Korea said it was looking at Trump’s comments. It said it hoped his relationship with Kim could help bring North Korea back to talks.
Trump’s decision comes after North Korea carried out new missile tests this month. The United Nations has banned North Korea from carrying out these tests.
Trump has cut military exercises with South Korea before. In 2018, he stopped them during talks with Kim and said the drills were too expensive.
Image source: File
Trump plans to give electric shock gloves to immigration officers
Donald Trump’s government plans to spend up to $20-million on electric shock gloves for US immigration officers.
The Department of Homeland Security says it could buy the gloves by March next year. They would be given to officers working for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as ICE.
The gloves can send electric shocks through a person’s skin. The company that makes them says the shocks are meant to distract someone and make it harder for them to move.
The gloves can produce up to 380 volts. The government says they would be used to help officers control difficult situations.
The plan has angered human rights groups. They fear the gloves could be used against immigrants and protesters.
ICE has already faced criticism over the way some officers have treated people. Critics have accused agents of using too much force and unfairly targeting people because of their race.
The company that makes the gloves says they are safe and do not cause injury. It also says they should not be used on some people, including small children, pregnant women and elderly people.
The planned deal could be worth between $10-million and $20-million.
Image source: File
Trump sued over paid early access to social media posts
US President Donald Trump has been sued over a paid service that gives some people early access to his Truth Social posts.
The service, called Truth API, charges up to $100,000 a month.
It gives paying customers faster access to posts from Trump and other senior US officials, including Vice President JD Vance and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
The lawsuit was filed by the Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation. They say the service is unfair and could allow Trump to profit from information he shares as president.
Trump has used Truth Social to announce major news about tariffs and the war with Iran. Some of those posts have moved stock and oil prices.
Trump Media says the service gives businesses quick access to posts that can move markets. The company said it already had more than 10 customers.
The lawsuit says Trump could personally benefit because he is the largest shareholder in Trump Media.
The groups want a court to stop the White House from using Truth Social as the only place for official announcements while some people pay to see them first.
Image source: File
Trump confirms secret plane switch after Iran threat
US President Donald Trump has confirmed that he secretly changed planes after leaving a Nato summit in Turkey last month because of a possible threat.
Trump said the Secret Service and the military told him to use a different plane. He said he followed their instructions.
Reports said Trump first boarded Air Force One in front of cameras on 8 July. He was then secretly moved off the plane in a catering truck and taken to a smaller military aircraft.
US officials said there was a real threat from Iran that a missile could be fired at Trump’s plane. One report said a person near the summit had been seen with a shoulder-fired missile.

Iran sent its proposal through Pakistani mediators, demanding an immediate end to the war, a stop to the US blockade of its ports, no further attacks and compensation for war damage. It also insisted on keeping control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump posted on Truth Social: “I have just read the response from Iran’s so-called ‘Representatives.’ I don’t like it. TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE.”
Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian warned his country would not back down. “We will never bow our heads before the enemy,” he said. “If talk of dialogue or negotiation arises, it does not mean surrender or retreat.”
The US had previously shared a 14-point plan with Iran that included stopping uranium enrichment, lifting sanctions and reopening the strait. Iran called it a “wish list.”
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu added to the pressure, saying Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium must be removed before the war can be considered over. “There are still enrichment sites that have to be dismantled,” he said.
Iran warned that any ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz would face “severe consequences” if they did not clear it with Tehran first. Kuwait said it shot down drones that entered its airspace. The UAE intercepted two Iranian drones. A ship near Qatar was hit by an unknown projectile.
More than 40 countries will meet on Monday to discuss protecting shipping in the strait once the fighting stops.

US and Iran exchange fire in biggest test of ceasefire yet
The US and Iran have traded strikes in the most serious clash since their ceasefire began a month ago, with both sides accusing the other of starting it.
The US military said Iranian forces fired missiles, drones and small boats at three American warships passing through the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday. It said all attacks were stopped and no US ships were hit. It then struck back, hitting Iranian missile launch sites, command centres and other military targets.
Iran said the US broke the ceasefire first by targeting an Iranian oil tanker and another ship near the strait. It said US strikes also hit civilian areas on the island of Qeshm, home to around 150,000 people, and along Iran’s southern coast.
Trump played down the clashes, calling them a “love tap.” “They trifled with us today,” he told reporters. “We blew them away.” He insisted the ceasefire was still holding and that a peace deal could still happen “any day.”
Oil prices climbed back above $101 a barrel after news of the strikes broke.
Reports before the fighting suggested the two sides were close to agreeing a one-page framework to end the war. But senior Iranian officials have been pushing back on key demands, with some reportedly wanting to drag out talks until closer to the US midterm elections in November, when they may be able to get a better deal.
Regional diplomats warned Iran not to push its luck. They said the current moment was a real chance to end the war and claim a victory, something that could slip away if full-scale fighting started again.
Pakistan’s prime minister had been optimistic just hours before the strikes, saying he firmly believed the ceasefire would become permanent.

Trump’s face is going on American passports

The new passport shows Trump’s image surrounded by the text of the Declaration of Independence and the American flag, with his signature printed in gold. Current US passports feature historical scenes such as the Moon landing and the Statue of Liberty.

Trump is also set to become the first sitting US president to have his signature printed on US banknotes.
